claims.claim: If a lookup costs about 1 ms, one core handles roughly 1,000/s (with a thin Python FastAPI/Flask layer)
claims.measured: Per 1 CPU: plaintext FastAPI 7,442 req/s, Flask (gthread) 4,031 req/s, Flask 1,732 req/s. CPU-bound test with about 1 ms of work per request: FastAPI 1,257 req/s, Flask 1,078 req/s, Flask-gthread 1,149 req/s
claims.why: Python servers doing about 1 ms of work per request measured about 1,050–1,260 req/s per core, which is close to the claimed ~1,000/s.

claims.claim: A C++ service would be fastest at runtime (compared with the Python options)
claims.measured: cpp-drogon 85,540 plaintext / 35,839 CPU req/s vs python-fastapi 7,442 / 1,257 and python-flask 1,732 / 1,078
claims.why: Drogon measured roughly 10–30 times faster than the Python stacks, and it had the highest CPU-test throughput of all servers.

claims.claim: With a memory-mapped index, start-up becomes close to instant and a restart costs seconds, not 3 minutes
claims.measured: Start-up: python-fastapi 895 ms, python-flask 996 ms, python-flask-gthread 606 ms
claims.why: The Python servers measured under 1 s to start, which fits 'close to instant' and 'seconds'.

claims.claim: A region returning 500,000 variants will not take 50 ms, because serialising JSON dominates
claims.why: The JSON test only serialises a tiny payload, so the cost of very large responses was not measured.
